title: The French Effect On ECB Policy
text:
The French Effect On ECB Policy

Cedric Gemehl

Gavekal Research | 28 Oct 2026

The market expects the European Central Bank’s bigwigs to leave their policy rate unchanged when they sit down in Frankfurt on Wednesday for their two-day meeting. But that does not mean the gathering will be easy or relaxed. On one front, inflation is above-target and accelerating, with the eurozone’s headline HICP price index up 3.8% year-on-year in September, versus 3.2% in August. On the other, sovereign stresses are mounting, especially in France where the 10-year OAT-bund yield spread has blown out to 156bp, from 90bp when the ECB’s governing council last met in early September. This confronts policymakers with a question: with the French bond market under pressure, can they continue to raise interest rates to combat inflation? The short answer is yes, they can. Although this does not necessarily mean they will. The distinction matters, because there are two different ways French bond market stresses can influence the ECB’s actions. The first is through the threat of financial market fragmentation, which the ECB can address independently of its monetary policy stance. The second is via the tightening of financial conditions implied by higher bond yields; this must be incorporated into the ECB’s monetary policy decisionmaking.
